keyVerseText: The sons also of Hezron, that were born unto him; Jerahmeel, and Ram, and Chelubai. Ram: Gr. Aram Chelubai: or, Caleb
rootMeaning: The name יְרַחְמְאֵל (Yᵉrachmᵉʼêl) is derived from the Hebrew root רָחַם (râcham), meaning to have compassion or love deeply, combined with אֵל (El), a common designation for God. Thus, the literal meaning of the name is "may God have compassion" or "God will be merciful." This etymology emphasizes not only divine mercy but also a tender, affectionate love that God extends to His people, enriching the common English gloss with a sense of intimate, compassionate care.
usageInScripture: The word יְרַחְמְאֵל appears eight times in Scripture, primarily as a proper name referring to three distinct individuals: the first son of Hezron and founder of the Jerahmeelite family, an officer under King Jehoiakim, and a Merarite Levite. Translations consistently render the name as Jerahmeel or related forms, highlighting its identity function. The four instances translated "of Jerahmeel" indicate a familial or tribal association, while the other occurrences affirm the personal name, demonstrating both individual and collective significance within Israel's history.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, the name יְרַחְמְאֵל reminds believers that God's compassion is foundational to His relationship with His people. As the name means "may God have pity," it reflects the hope and trust placed in God's mercy throughout Scripture. This emphasis on divine compassion aligns with the gospel message, where God's loving mercy is fully revealed in Christ. Recognizing this name within the biblical narrative encourages believers to rely on God's tender affection and to mirror that compassion in their own lives, affirming God's covenant faithfulness and care.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Chronicles 2:9, the text lists Jerahmeel among the sons of Hezron, establishing his role as a progenitor of a significant family line. The presence of the name יְרַחְמְאֵל here underscores the heritage of God’s compassionate care extended through generations. By naming this son "may God have compassion," the verse connects the familial lineage to the ongoing reality of divine mercy and blessing upon Judah's descendants.
